claims.statement: Talon treats cron and background-result delivery as unattended: the host withholds approval and authorization handlers, and the runtime auto-denies approval interrupts for cron or background delivery even if an approval handler is injected.

Detached Talon background subagents clear the authorization handler and approval-operator state before work, retain required copied context under a new task thread, and convert an unresolved tool-approval interrupt into a result saying the protected action has not run.

For a cron turn, Talon runs `task` and `start_async_task` inline rather than creating a background job, hides worker-management tools, and uses a separate queued four-slot inline semaphore with a ten-minute per-delegation default timeout.

Talon clamps detached and inline subagent output to answer text with a 64,000-character maximum, excluding non-text message blocks; ordinary failures and timeouts return safe summaries without tool arguments or exception payloads instead of escaping the delegation path.

`LocalContextMiddleware` keeps `untrusted` MCP servers out of the model-facing inventory and sanitizes, single-lines, and bounds MCP errors and tracing-project names before prompt insertion; this prompt framing does not authenticate or contain an enabled integration.

Talon OAuth does not initiate a channel authorization flow without a current authorization handler, invocation, and attempt; scheduled and background work instead receive a remediation error, while a channel flow binds the server, invocation, expiry, and redirect URI.

Talon's OAuth client uses a public-HTTPS SSRF-safe transport that ignores environment proxies and refuses redirects; endpoint resolution is separately bounded, and device-flow endpoints must share the authorization-server origin.

Talon stores MCP tokens in per-owner directories and files with modes 0700 and 0600, serializes read-modify-write updates under a lock, atomically replaces the token file, and retains a prior refresh token when a refresh response omits one.

Talon local subagents are compiled with fresh context and explicit tool attachment: `fork` is rejected, dynamically selected tools must be unique catalog names, approval middleware includes only enabled attached tools, and opaque precompiled local subagents are refused whenever an approval policy exists.

A fresh per-task subagent turns an unresolved approval interrupt into the result that the protected action has not run, and extracts only textual message content, so reasoning-only blocks do not become a delegated result.
Talon's sandbox is opt-in for shell and file tools; MCP, web, and channel media handling remain host-side, so sandbox selection is not a multi-tenant boundary.

Talon's Claude Code, Codex, and dcode session bridges are disabled by default and operator-only; dcode and Claude constrain discovery to same-user sockets in private directories, while Codex queues ordinary target-session turns and does not enforce Talon's relayed-message framing.

The release workflow isolates untrusted build work from publishing: build has read-only repository permissions, while TestPyPI and PyPI publication run in the `release` environment with only `id-token: write`, verify downloaded artifact checksums, and do not check out source.

GitHub workflow credential-scoping tests enforce package-conditional integration secret wiring, retain the disabled release integration wiring, and require the OpenWiki job to use its dedicated environment and narrowly scoped GitHub App token after the OpenWiki run.

Talon frames inbound documents as JSON-encoded path notices that call the attachment and path untrusted rather than inlining bytes, limits model image blocks to locally readable image inputs no larger than 5 MiB, and replaces attachment failure details with a generic unavailable notice.

For remote sandbox execution, Talon stages inbound documents into a UUID-named `.talon/attachments` backend path only after resolving the source beneath configured inbound media roots, rejecting unsafe or oversized non-regular files with no-follow file access; it replaces metadata with the backend-readable path and reports staging failure only as unavailable media.

Talon's request-scoped `send_file` reads through the configured agent backend only for a current chat turn, refuses subagents, sanitizes the recipient filename, and stages upload bytes in a fresh 0700 directory as a 0600 no-follow file that is removed after sending; channel transport errors are returned to the model without their details.

Outbound media validation can require a trusted root: it strictly resolves local paths, rejects traversal, URL, home-directory and symlink escapes, requires a regular file, and checks inferred category and configured size before an adapter sends media.
